items.stem: Our class ____ a science project last Friday.

explain.why: 'last Friday' is a finished past time, but 'completes' is simple present.
'last Friday' is already past, so the future 'will complete' cannot be used.
'is completing' is present continuous, but 'last Friday' needs the simple past.

solution: Our class completed a science project last Friday.
'last Friday' marks a finished time in the past, so use the simple past 'completed'.

items.stem: Look! The pupils ____ towards the school bus.

explain.why: 'Look!' signals something happening now, so the simple past 'ran' does not fit.
'Look!' shows the action is happening now, so past continuous 'were running' is wrong.
'Look!' points to an action happening now, which needs the present continuous, not the simple present for habits.

solution: Look! The pupils are running towards the school bus.
'Look!' signals an action in progress now, so use the present continuous 'are running'.

items.stem: My father ____ to work by MRT every morning.

explain.why: 'has gone' means he has left and is not here; it does not describe a daily habit.
'every morning' shows a habit, which uses the simple present, not the present continuous.
'every morning' with the present 'My father' is a habit now, not a finished past event.

solution: My father goes to work by MRT every morning.
'every morning' shows a habit, so use the simple present 'goes'.

items.stem: Ben ____ his lunch when the fire alarm rang.

explain.why: 'rang' is past, so the action in progress at that time must be past continuous, not 'is eating'.
'were' is plural, but the subject 'Ben' is singular.
'eats' is simple present, but 'rang' puts the story in the past.

solution: Ben was eating his lunch when the fire alarm rang.
A longer past action interrupted by a shorter one uses the past continuous: 'was eating' when the alarm rang.

items.stem: By the time we arrived, the film ____ already started.

explain.why: 'did' must be followed by the base form 'start', but the sentence has 'started'.
'the film' is singular, so 'have' does not agree; the past perfect also needs 'had'.
'arrived' is past, so the earlier action needs past perfect 'had started', not present perfect 'has started'.

solution: By the time we arrived, the film had already started.
'By the time we arrived' needs the past perfect 'had started' for the earlier action.

items.stem: Tomorrow, our teacher ____ us the results of the spelling test.

explain.why: 'has given' is present perfect and cannot go with the future time 'Tomorrow'.
'Tomorrow' points to the future, so the simple past 'gave' is wrong.
'was giving' is past continuous, but 'Tomorrow' needs a future form.

solution: Tomorrow, our teacher will give us the results of the spelling test.
'Tomorrow' needs the future 'will give'.

items.stem: Aisha ____ in this HDB block since she was born.

explain.why: 'since she was born' links the past to now, so the present perfect 'has lived' is needed, not the simple past.
'since' with a starting point needs a perfect tense; simple present 'lives' does not fit.
'is living' is present continuous and does not combine with 'since' to show a period up to now.

solution: Aisha has lived in this HDB block since she was born.
'since' + a past starting point takes the present perfect 'has lived'.

items.stem: ____ you finished your homework yet?

explain.why: 'Did' must be followed by the base form 'finish', but the sentence has 'finished'.
'Will' must be followed by the base form 'finish', but the sentence has 'finished'.
'you' takes 'have', not 'has'.

solution: Have you finished your homework yet?
'yet' with 'finished' needs the present perfect, so 'Have you finished'.

items.stem: The bus ____ by the time Wei Ling reached the stop.

explain.why: 'is leaving' is present continuous, which clashes with the past 'reached'.
'reached' is past, so the earlier action needs past perfect, not present perfect 'has left'.
'would leave' looks forward from the past; here the bus left before she reached the stop.

solution: The bus had already left by the time Wei Ling reached the stop.
'By the time' + simple past takes the past perfect for the earlier event: 'had already left'.

items.stem: Since the new library opened, the number of visitors ____ steadily.

explain.why: 'The number' is singular, so 'has' is needed, not 'have'.
'since' needs a perfect tense; simple present continuous 'is rising' does not connect to the starting point.
'Since the library opened' covers a period up to now, so past continuous 'was rising' does not fit.

solution: Since the new library opened, the number of visitors has been rising steadily.
'Since' + a past event needs the present perfect, and 'the number' is singular: 'has been rising'.

items.stem: Mrs Tan ____ at this school for twenty years when she retired last month.

explain.why: 'would teach' does not show a completed period of twenty years before she retired.
'for twenty years' before another past event needs a perfect form, not past continuous.
'retired last month' is past, so present perfect continuous 'has been teaching' does not fit.

solution: Mrs Tan had been teaching at this school for twenty years when she retired last month.
A period lasting up to an earlier past moment uses the past perfect continuous: 'had been teaching'.

items.stem: While I ____ for the bus, it started to rain heavily.

explain.why: 'started' is past, so present perfect continuous 'have been waiting' clashes with it.
'would wait' does not show an action in progress when the rain started.
'started' is past, so simple present 'wait' is inconsistent.

solution: While I was waiting for the bus, it started to rain heavily.
'While' with a past interruption takes the past continuous 'was waiting'.

items.stem: Ravi ____ his keys, so he could not enter the house.

explain.why: 'could not enter' is past, so the earlier loss needs 'had lost', not 'has lost'.
'loses' is simple present, but 'could not enter' is past.
'was losing' describes a process, but the keys were already gone before he reached the door.

solution: Ravi had lost his keys, so he could not enter the house.
The loss happened before 'could not enter', so use the past perfect 'had lost'.

items.stem: How long ____ you been learning the violin?

explain.why: 'did' cannot be followed by 'been learning'; 'been' needs 'have' before it.
'will been' is ungrammatical; 'been learning' needs 'have' before it.
'you' takes 'have', not 'has'.

solution: How long have you been learning the violin?
'been learning' is present perfect continuous, so the auxiliary is 'have' after 'you'.

items.stem: I ____ my cousin tomorrow, so I cannot come for the CCA session.

explain.why: 'was visiting' is past, but the plan is for tomorrow.
'tomorrow' is in the future, so simple past 'visited' is wrong.
'tomorrow' needs a future form; present perfect 'have visited' is wrong.

solution: I am visiting my cousin tomorrow, so I cannot come for the CCA session.
A fixed plan for the future can use the present continuous: 'am visiting ... tomorrow'.

items.stem: My brother ____ the guitar for three years now.

explain.why: 'for three years now' shows a period up to now, so simple present 'plays' does not fit.
'My brother' is singular, so 'has' is needed, not 'have'.
'now' links to the present, so past perfect 'had played' is wrong.

solution: My brother has been playing the guitar for three years now.
'for three years now' needs the present perfect continuous 'has been playing'.

items.stem: By next June, Kai Wen ____ in this choir for four years.

explain.why: 'would sing' cannot express the total length of time reached by next June.
'By next June' is future; 'had been singing' belongs to the past.
'would have been singing' is an unreal past form and does not give the real total reached by next June.

solution: By next June, Kai Wen will have been singing in this choir for four years.
'By next June' + a length of time takes the future perfect (continuous): 'will have been singing'.

items.stem: The museum guide explained that the ship ____ in 1850 and had sailed to Singapore many times since.

explain.why: 'in 1850' is a fixed past time, which cannot be used with the present perfect.
'in 1850' is a past date, and the clause after 'explained' is in the past, so 'is built' is inconsistent.
The ship did not do the building; it needs the passive 'was built'.

solution: The museum guide explained that the ship was built in 1850 and had sailed to Singapore many times since.
A ship is built by people, so the passive 'was built', with the past date 'in 1850'.

items.stem: Although it ____ heavily since morning, the football match went on as planned.

explain.why: 'went on' is past, so present perfect continuous 'has been raining' is inconsistent.
'since morning' needs a perfect form; 'was raining' cannot take 'since'.
'since morning' cannot go with the simple past 'rained'.

solution: Although it had been raining heavily since morning, the football match went on as planned.
'since morning' before a past event ('went on') needs the past perfect continuous 'had been raining'.

items.stem: The runner collapsed at the finish line because he ____ without stopping for two hours.

explain.why: 'is running' is present, but the whole sentence is in the past.
'runs' is simple present and clashes with 'collapsed'.
'collapsed' is past, so present perfect continuous 'has been running' does not match.

solution: The runner collapsed at the finish line because he had been running without stopping for two hours.
A long action before a past event takes the past perfect continuous: 'had been running'.

items.stem: Next week, when the P6 pupils ____ their oral exam, they will take a short break.

explain.why: 'will' is not used inside a 'when' clause about the future.
After 'when' for a future event, the verb stays in a present form; 'will' is not used inside the clause.
'would finish' is a past-based form and does not fit 'Next week ... will take'.

solution: Next week, when the P6 pupils have finished their oral exam, they will take a short break.
After 'when' in a future sentence, use a present form; 'have finished' shows it is done first.

items.stem: Whenever the haze got bad, my grandfather ____ the windows and switched on the air purifier.

explain.why: 'got' and 'switched' are past, so 'will close' is inconsistent.
'would' must be followed by the base form 'close', not 'closed'.
A repeated habit in the past uses 'would', not past perfect, which shows an earlier action.

solution: Whenever the haze got bad, my grandfather would close the windows and switched on the air purifier.
'Whenever ... got' describes a repeated past habit, so use 'would close'.

items.stem: Jia Hui ____ the piano since Primary 3, and she is now preparing for her Grade 5 exam.

explain.why: 'since' needs the present perfect; simple present 'plays' cannot take 'since'.
'is now preparing' is present, so past perfect 'had played' is inconsistent.
'since Primary 3' and 'is now' need a perfect tense, not the simple past.

solution: Jia Hui has played the piano since Primary 3, and she is now preparing for her Grade 5 exam.
'since Primary 3' up to the present takes the present perfect 'has played'.

items.stem: I wish I ____ more attention during yesterday's lesson.

explain.why: 'wish' is followed by a past form, not present perfect 'have paid'.
A wish about the past ('yesterday') needs the past perfect, not simple past.
'would pay' expresses a wish about the future, not a regret about yesterday.

solution: I wish I had paid more attention during yesterday's lesson.
A wish about a past event takes the past perfect: 'I wish I had paid'.

items.stem: It was only after the guests had left that Mum realised she ____ to buy dessert.

explain.why: 'realised' is past, so present perfect 'has forgotten' is inconsistent.
'would forget' looks forward; the forgetting happened before she realised.
'was forgetting' shows a process, but the forgetting was a completed earlier event.

solution: It was only after the guests had left that Mum realised she had forgotten to buy dessert.
The forgetting came before 'realised', so use the past perfect 'had forgotten'.

items.stem: The school fair will be held ____ Saturday.

explain.why: 'in' is used for months, years and parts of a day, not a named day.
'by' means 'no later than', not the day on which an event is held.
'at' is used for clock times and points, not for days of the week.

solution: The school fair will be held on Saturday.
Days of the week take 'on': on Saturday.

items.stem: The accident happened ____ midnight.

explain.why: 'by midnight' means 'before midnight', not the moment it happened.
'on' is used with days and dates, not with an exact time like midnight.
'in' is used with longer periods such as 'in the morning', not an exact time.

solution: The accident happened at midnight.
A point in time such as midnight takes 'at'.

items.stem: She has been learning the piano ____ three years.

explain.why: 'since' needs a starting point such as 'Primary 3', but 'three years' is a length of time.
'at' cannot introduce a length of time.
'during' needs a named period (during the holidays), not a number of years.

solution: She has been learning the piano for three years.
A length of time ('three years') takes 'for'.

items.stem: He has been absent ____ Monday.

explain.why: 'at' is used for clock times, not for a starting day.
'during' needs a named period or event, not a starting day like 'Monday'.
'for' needs a length of time such as 'three days', but 'Monday' is a starting point.

solution: He has been absent since Monday.
A starting point in time ('Monday') takes 'since'.

items.stem: Wei Jie is very good ____ drawing.

explain.why: 'good on' does not describe a skill.
The adjective 'good' takes 'at' for a skill, not 'in'.
'good with' is used for handling people or things, not for a skill like drawing.

solution: Wei Jie is very good at drawing.
'good at' + a skill or activity.

items.stem: I am afraid ____ spiders.

explain.why: The adjective 'afraid' takes 'of', not 'from'.
'afraid for' means worried about someone's safety, not a fear of spiders.
'afraid to' needs a verb after it, not a noun like 'spiders'.

solution: I am afraid of spiders.
'afraid of' + the thing feared.

items.stem: Our team is responsible ____ keeping the classroom tidy.

explain.why: 'responsible to' means answerable to a person, not in charge of a task.
'responsible with' is not the usual collocation for a duty.
'responsible' takes 'for' when it names the job, not 'of'.

solution: Our team is responsible for keeping the classroom tidy.
'responsible for' + the duty.

items.stem: I have been looking forward ____ the school camp.

explain.why: 'look forward on' is not an English phrase.
The phrase is 'look forward to', not 'look forward for'.
'look forward at' is not an English phrase.

solution: I have been looking forward to the school camp.
'look forward to' + a noun or gerund.

items.stem: The hawker was fined ____ selling food without a licence.

explain.why: 'fined of' is not used; the reason for a fine takes 'for'.
'fined on' is not used for the offence.
'fined with' is not used for the offence.

solution: The hawker was fined for selling food without a licence.
'fined for' + the offence.

items.stem: Please return the library books ____ next Monday.

explain.why: 'on' names a day an event happens, and 'on next Monday' is not used; a deadline needs 'by'.
'during' needs a period of time that something happens within, not a deadline day.
'until' is used for an action that continues up to a time, but returning is a one-time action with a deadline.

solution: Please return the library books by next Monday.
A deadline ('no later than next Monday') takes 'by'.

items.stem: The cat hid ____ the sofa and the wall.

explain.why: 'beside' means next to one thing, but the cat is in the gap between two.
'among' is used for three or more things; here there are only two, the sofa and the wall.
'against' means pressed on something and does not fit two objects with 'and'.

solution: The cat hid between the sofa and the wall.
Two objects joined by 'and' take 'between'.

items.stem: She cut the cake ____ a knife.

explain.why: 'by' is used for means like 'by bus', not for a tool.
'in' does not show the tool used.
'through' means passing from one side to another, not using a tool.

solution: She cut the cake with a knife.
A tool or instrument takes 'with'.

items.stem: Ali insisted ____ paying for everyone's drinks at the hawker centre.

explain.why: 'insist for' is not used in English.
'insist with' is not used in English.
'insist' takes 'on' before a gerund, not 'to'.

solution: Ali insisted on paying for everyone's drinks at the hawker centre.
'insist on' + gerund.

items.stem: Whether the school camp can go ahead after weeks of planning depends entirely ____ the weather.

explain.why: 'depend with' is not used in English.
'depend' takes 'on', not 'from'.
'depend to' is not used in English.

solution: Whether the school camp can go ahead after weeks of planning depends entirely on the weather.
'depend on' + the factor.

items.stem: Despite the heavy rain, the volunteers carried on ____ clearing the drains.

explain.why: 'carry on from' means continuing from a point, not continuing with a task.
'carry on for' is not used for continuing a task.
'carry on by clearing' would mean the way they continued, not the same task.

solution: Despite the heavy rain, the volunteers carried on with clearing the drains.
'carry on with' + the task.

items.stem: Instead ____ complaining about the long queue, Mei Xin chatted with the stallholder.

explain.why: The phrase is 'instead of', not 'instead for'.
The phrase is 'instead of', not 'instead to'.
The phrase is 'instead of', not 'instead from'.

solution: Instead of complaining about the long queue, Mei Xin chatted with the stallholder.
'instead of' + gerund.

items.stem: I would like to apologise ____ keeping you waiting.

explain.why: 'apologise from' is not used; the fault takes 'for'.
'apologise' takes 'for' before the reason, not 'of'.
'apologise at' is not used for the reason.

solution: I would like to apologise for keeping you waiting.
'apologise for' + the fault.

items.stem: Tom was accused ____ cheating, though he had done nothing wrong.

explain.why: 'accused' takes 'of' before the offence, not 'for'.
'accused with' is not used; 'charged with' is a different phrase.
'accused on' is not used for the offence.

solution: Tom was accused of cheating, though he had done nothing wrong.
'accuse someone of' + the offence.

items.stem: Pupils must refrain ____ running along the corridors.

explain.why: 'refrain at' is not used in English.
'refrain to' is not used; the verb takes 'from' before a gerund.
'refrain with' is not used in English; 'refrain' takes 'from'.

solution: Pupils must refrain from running along the corridors.
'refrain from' + gerund.

items.stem: Mei Ling enjoys ____ in the school choir.

explain.why: 'sang' is a past tense and cannot follow 'enjoys'.
'enjoy' is followed by a gerund (-ing), not 'to' + verb.
'enjoy' needs the -ing form; the base form 'sing' is ungrammatical here.

solution: Mei Ling enjoys singing in the school choir.
'enjoy' + gerund: enjoys singing.

items.stem: We decided ____ the zoo on Saturday.

explain.why: 'decide' is followed by 'to' + verb, not a gerund.
'decided' must be followed by an infinitive, not a past tense.
'decide' needs 'to' before the verb.

solution: We decided to visit the zoo on Saturday.
'decide' + to-infinitive: decided to visit.

items.stem: My mother asked me ____ the rubbish out.

explain.why: 'asked me' cannot be followed by a past tense verb.
After 'to' the base form is used, not -ing, so 'to taking' is wrong.
'asked me' is followed by 'to' + verb, not -ing.

solution: My mother asked me to take the rubbish out.
'ask someone' + to-infinitive: asked me to take.

items.stem: Jun is looking forward to ____ his grandparents.

explain.why: 'look forward to' already has 'to'; another 'to' is not added.
'to' here is a preposition, so the verb after it must be -ing.
A preposition cannot be followed by a past tense verb.

solution: Jun is looking forward to seeing his grandparents.
'look forward to' + gerund: looking forward to seeing.

items.stem: I am tired of ____ the same food every day.

explain.why: After the preposition 'of', the verb takes -ing.
'tired of' is followed by a gerund, not 'to' + verb.
A preposition cannot be followed by a past tense verb.

solution: I am tired of eating the same food every day.
Preposition + gerund: tired of eating.

items.stem: Would you mind ____ the window?

explain.why: 'Would you mind' needs the -ing form.
'mind' cannot be followed by a past tense verb.
'mind' is followed by a gerund, not 'to' + verb.

solution: Would you mind closing the window?
'mind' + gerund: Would you mind closing...?

items.stem: The boys were seen ____ in the playground after the bell.

explain.why: A finite verb 'plays' cannot follow 'were seen'.
After 'to' the verb must be in the base form, so 'to played' is wrong.
'were seen played' is not a correct passive pattern; it needs 'playing'.

solution: The boys were seen playing in the playground after the bell.
'be seen' + -ing shows an action in progress: were seen playing.

items.stem: The vase, ____ by a naughty puppy, lay in pieces on the floor.

explain.why: The vase was broken by the puppy, so the passive participle is needed, not -ing.
The base form 'break' cannot follow a noun here.
'to break' shows purpose and does not say who broke the vase.

solution: The vase, broken by a naughty puppy, lay in pieces on the floor.
A past participle gives a passive meaning: the vase, broken by a puppy.

items.stem: My teacher made us ____ the school song three times.

explain.why: After 'made us' the base form is needed, not the past tense.
'made us' is followed by the base verb, not -ing.
'make' someone do something takes the bare verb, without 'to'.

solution: My teacher made us sing the school song three times.
'make someone' + bare infinitive: made us sing.

items.stem: Rina was too shy ____ her hand to answer the question.

explain.why: 'too + adjective' needs 'to' before the verb.
'too shy' is followed by 'to' + verb, not -ing.
After 'to' the verb must be in the base form, so 'to raised' is wrong.

solution: Rina was too shy to raise her hand to answer the question.
'too + adjective + to-infinitive': too shy to raise.

items.stem: We could not help ____ when the clown slipped on the banana skin.

explain.why: 'cannot help' is followed by -ing, not 'to' + verb.
'could not help' needs the -ing form.
'help' cannot be followed by a past tense verb.

solution: We could not help laughing when the clown slipped on the banana skin.
'cannot help' + gerund: could not help laughing.

items.stem: Having ____ his homework, Jun Jie went out to play basketball.

explain.why: 'Having finishing' is not a correct form; 'having' takes the past participle.
'Having been finished' is passive, but Jun Jie did the finishing.
'Having' must be followed by a past participle.

solution: Having finished his homework, Jun Jie went out to play basketball.
'Having' + past participle shows the earlier action: Having finished...

items.stem: The coach suggested ____ an extra training session before the match.

explain.why: 'suggested' cannot be followed directly by a past tense verb.
'suggest' is followed by a gerund, not 'to' + verb.
'suggested have' is wrong; 'suggest' needs the -ing form here.

solution: The coach suggested having an extra training session before the match.
'suggest' + gerund: suggested having.

items.stem: The old shophouse, ____ in 1920, is now a museum.

explain.why: The shophouse did not build itself, so the passive participle 'built' is needed.
'was built' would add a second finite verb between commas, making the sentence ungrammatical.
'build' is the base form; the passive meaning needs the past participle 'built'.

solution: The old shophouse, built in 1920, is now a museum.
A past participle phrase gives a passive meaning: the shophouse, built in 1920.

items.stem: I would rather ____ in the shade than play in this heat.

explain.why: 'would rather' is followed by the base form, not the past tense, for a present preference.
'would rather' needs the base form, not -ing.
'would rather' is followed by the bare infinitive, without 'to'.

solution: I would rather sit in the shade than play in this heat.
'would rather' + bare infinitive: would rather sit.

items.stem: Rain or shine, the hawker is used to ____ up at four in the morning.

explain.why: 'is used to' already contains 'to'; another 'to' is not added.
In 'be used to', 'to' is a preposition, so the verb must be -ing.
'used to' (be accustomed) cannot be followed by a past tense verb.

solution: Rain or shine, the hawker is used to waking up at four in the morning.
'be used to' + gerund: is used to waking up.

items.stem: Not ____ what to say, Hui Min kept quiet.

explain.why: A participle phrase at the start needs -ing, not the base form.
'known' is passive; Hui Min was the one who did not know.
'Not to know' changes the meaning to a purpose and does not explain why she kept quiet.

solution: Not knowing what to say, Hui Min kept quiet.
A participial phrase of reason takes -ing: Not knowing...

items.stem: The boys ____ playing football on the field.

explain.why: 'was' goes with a singular subject, but 'The boys' is plural.
'has' cannot be followed by 'playing' as a continuous form; 'are playing' is needed.
'is' needs a singular subject, but the subject here is 'The boys'.

solution: The boys are playing football on the field.
'The boys' is plural, so use 'are'.

items.stem: Everyone in my class ____ a library card.

explain.why: 'having' is not a finite verb, so the sentence has no main verb.
'Everyone' is singular, so it takes 'has', not 'have'.
'are' cannot be followed by 'a library card' and does not agree with 'Everyone'.

solution: Everyone in my class has a library card.
'Everyone' is singular, so 'has'.

items.stem: My brother and my sister ____ the same tuition teacher.

explain.why: Two subjects joined by 'and' make a plural subject, so 'has' is wrong.
'does' is an auxiliary and does not mean 'possess' here.
'is' cannot link to 'the same tuition teacher' as an action verb, and it is singular.

solution: My brother and my sister have the same tuition teacher.
'My brother and my sister' is a plural subject, so 'have'.

items.stem: The water in those bottles ____ still cold.

explain.why: 'be' is not a finite verb and does not agree with 'The water'; 'is' is needed.
'were' is plural; the subject is 'The water'.
'are' agrees with the nearby 'bottles', but the subject is 'The water', which is singular.

solution: The water in those bottles is still cold.
The subject is 'The water' (singular), so 'is', not agreeing with 'bottles'.

items.stem: The news about the school trip ____ exciting.

explain.why: 'news' is treated as singular, so 'were' is wrong.
'news' looks plural but is an uncountable noun and takes a singular verb.
'be' is not a finite verb and does not agree with 'The news'; 'is' is needed.

solution: The news about the school trip is exciting.
'news' is singular, so 'is'.

items.stem: Neither Ali nor his friends ____ finished the project.

explain.why: With 'neither ... nor', the verb agrees with the nearer subject 'his friends', which is plural.
'were' cannot be followed by 'finished' to form the perfect tense; 'have finished' is needed.
'was' cannot be followed by 'finished' to form a perfect tense.

solution: Neither Ali nor his friends have finished the project.
'neither ... nor' follows the nearer subject: 'his friends' is plural, so 'have'.

items.stem: Each of the P6 pupils ____ a copy of the revision notes.

explain.why: 'are' does not suit 'a copy of the notes' and does not agree with 'Each'.
'do' is an auxiliary and cannot mean 'possess' here.
'Each' is singular, even though 'pupils' comes right before the blank.

solution: Each of the P6 pupils has a copy of the revision notes.
'Each of' + plural noun takes a singular verb: has.

items.stem: A number of pupils ____ absent today because of the flu.

explain.why: 'has been' is singular; 'a number of pupils' is plural.
'A number of' means 'several', so the verb is plural.
'was' is singular, but 'a number of pupils' is plural; the time 'today' also needs present.

solution: A number of pupils are absent today because of the flu.
'A number of' + plural noun takes a plural verb: are.

items.stem: The number of pupils in the choir ____ increased this year.

explain.why: 'The number of' is singular, so it takes 'has', not 'have'.
'were' cannot be followed by 'increased' to form a perfect tense.
'are' cannot be followed by 'increased' to form a perfect tense.

solution: The number of pupils in the choir has increased this year.
'The number of' is singular, so 'has increased'.

items.stem: The police ____ questioning two men outside the shopping centre.

explain.why: 'has been' is singular; 'the police' is plural.
'police' takes a plural verb, and 'was' is singular.
'police' is always plural, so 'is' is wrong.

solution: The police are questioning two men outside the shopping centre.
'The police' is plural, so 'are'.

items.stem: The quality of the cookies sold at the school fair ____ improved a great deal.

explain.why: 'are' cannot be followed by 'improved' to form the perfect tense.
'have' agrees with the nearby 'cookies', but the subject is 'The quality', which is singular.
'were' cannot be followed by 'improved' to form the perfect tense.

solution: The quality of the cookies sold at the school fair has improved a great deal.
The subject is 'The quality' (singular), so 'has improved'.

items.stem: Either the teacher or the prefects ____ going to announce the winners.

explain.why: With 'either ... or', the verb agrees with the nearer subject 'the prefects', which is plural.
'was' is singular, and the tense does not match 'going to announce'.
'has' cannot be followed by 'going' as a continuous form.

solution: Either the teacher or the prefects are going to announce the winners.
'either ... or' agrees with the nearer subject: 'prefects' is plural, so 'are'.

items.stem: The list of items to bring for the camp ____ pinned on the notice board for a week, so check it before you pack.

explain.why: 'are' agrees with the nearby 'items', and 'for a week' needs a perfect tense.
'were' is plural, but the subject is 'The list' (singular).
'have been' agrees with the nearby 'items', but the subject is 'The list', which is singular.

solution: The list of items to bring for the camp has been pinned on the notice board for a week, so check it before you pack.
The subject is 'The list' (singular), so 'has been pinned'.

items.stem: Not only the pupils but also their form teacher ____ excited about the camp for weeks.

explain.why: 'were' is plural, and 'for weeks' needs a perfect tense.
With 'not only ... but also', the verb agrees with the nearer subject 'their form teacher', which is singular.
'are' is plural, and 'for weeks' needs a perfect tense.

solution: Not only the pupils but also their form teacher has been excited about the camp for weeks.
'not only ... but also' agrees with the nearer subject (singular): has been.

items.stem: The teacher, together with her P6 pupils, ____ at the MRT station since 7 a.m.

explain.why: 'together with her P6 pupils' does not make the subject plural; the subject is only 'The teacher'.
'since 7 a.m.' needs a perfect tense, not past continuous.
'since 7 a.m.' needs a perfect tense, not simple present continuous.

solution: The teacher, together with her P6 pupils, has been waiting at the MRT station since 7 a.m.
'together with' does not change the subject; 'since' needs the perfect: has been waiting.

items.stem: There is ____ juice left in the jug.

explain.why: 'a number of' goes with plural countable nouns, but 'juice' is uncountable.
'many' is used with countable plural nouns, not with uncountable 'juice'.
'a few' is used with countable nouns, but 'juice' is uncountable.

solution: There is a little juice left in the jug.
'juice' is uncountable, so 'a little'.

items.stem: How ____ pupils are there in your class?

explain.why: 'little' goes with uncountable nouns, not 'pupils'.
'much' is for uncountable nouns, but 'pupils' is countable.
'a little' goes with uncountable nouns, not 'pupils'.

solution: How many pupils are there in your class?
'pupils' is countable, so 'How many'.

items.stem: Could I have ____ apple from the basket, please?

explain.why: 'apple' begins with a vowel sound, so it takes 'an', not 'a'.
'many' needs a plural noun, but 'apple' is singular.
'few' needs a plural noun, but 'apple' is singular.

solution: Could I have an apple from the basket, please?
Before a vowel sound, use 'an': an apple.

items.stem: She drank ____ water after the run.

explain.why: 'many' is used with countable plural nouns, not uncountable 'water'.
'few' is used with countable plural nouns, not uncountable 'water'.
'a' is used before a singular countable noun, but 'water' is uncountable.

solution: She drank some water after the run.
'water' is uncountable, so 'some'.

items.stem: We have ____ time left, so we must hurry.

explain.why: 'a few' goes with countable nouns, but 'time' here is uncountable.
'few' goes with countable nouns, but 'time' here is uncountable.
'several' goes with plural countable nouns, but 'time' here is uncountable.

solution: We have little time left, so we must hurry.
'time' is uncountable and the meaning is 'not enough', so 'little'.

items.stem: There were so ____ people at the hawker centre that we had to wait for a table.

explain.why: 'much' is for uncountable nouns, but 'people' is a countable plural.
'little' is for uncountable nouns, and it would mean there were hardly any people.
'so few' would mean there were hardly any people, which does not explain the wait.

solution: There were so many people at the hawker centre that we had to wait for a table.
'people' is countable and the meaning is 'a large number', so 'so many'.

items.stem: He has ____ friends, so he often feels lonely.

explain.why: 'a little' goes with uncountable nouns, but 'friends' is countable.
'any' is used mainly in negatives and questions, not in a positive statement like this.
'a few' means some, which is positive; 'feels lonely' needs the negative 'few'.

solution: He has few friends, so he often feels lonely.
'friends' is countable and the meaning is 'hardly any', so 'few'.

items.stem: We have ____ sugar left, so we can still bake a small cake.

explain.why: 'few' goes with countable nouns, but 'sugar' is uncountable.
'a few' goes with countable nouns, but 'sugar' is uncountable.
'a number of' goes with plural countable nouns, but 'sugar' is uncountable.

solution: We have a little sugar left, so we can still bake a small cake.
'sugar' is uncountable and 'can still bake' is positive, so 'a little'.

items.stem: I have two pens, but ____ of them works.

explain.why: 'none' is used for three or more things; here there are only two pens.
'either of them works' means at least one works, which contradicts 'but'.
'everyone of them' is not used, and it would contradict 'but'.

solution: I have two pens, but neither of them works.
For two things, 'neither of them' means 'not one and not the other'.

items.stem: ____ pupil in the class must hand in the form by Friday.

explain.why: 'Several' needs a plural noun, but 'pupil' is singular.
'Many' needs a plural noun, but 'pupil' is singular.
'All' needs a plural noun, but 'pupil' is singular.

solution: Every pupil in the class must hand in the form by Friday.
'pupil' is singular, so 'Every'.

items.stem: The more homework Kiara had, ____ time she had to play.

explain.why: 'the least' is a superlative, but the sentence compares two changes.
'fewer' is used with countable nouns, but 'time' is uncountable.
'The more ..., the less ...' needs 'the' before the second comparative.

solution: The more homework Kiara had, the less time she had to play.
'time' is uncountable, so 'the less' in 'the more ..., the less ...'.

items.stem: Hardly ____ pupils came to the extra class because of the rain, so it was cancelled.

explain.why: 'hardly' is already negative, so adding 'no' makes a double negative.
'a little' goes with uncountable nouns, but 'pupils' is countable.
'hardly a few' is not used; 'hardly' goes with 'any'.

solution: Hardly any pupils came to the extra class because of the rain, so it was cancelled.
'hardly' is followed by 'any': Hardly any pupils came.

items.stem: I cannot find ____ my pen or my ruler.

explain.why: 'any' does not combine with 'or' to join two named items.
'both' is used with 'and', not 'or'.
'cannot ... neither' makes a double negative.

solution: I cannot find either my pen or my ruler.
'either ... or' joins two items after a negative: cannot find either ... or ....

items.stem: Not all the answers were correct; ____ were wrong.

explain.why: 'no' would say none were wrong, which contradicts 'Not all'.
'any' is used mainly in negatives and questions, but this is a positive statement.
'every' needs a singular noun, and 'every were' is ungrammatical.

solution: Not all the answers were correct; some were wrong.
'Not all were correct' means some were wrong, so 'some'.

items.stem: We spent so ____ money on the gift that we had none left for the card.

explain.why: 'many' is used with countable nouns, but 'money' is uncountable.
'so such money' is ungrammatical; 'such' cannot follow 'so'.
'too' would need 'to' after it, not 'that'.

solution: We spent so much money on the gift that we had none left for the card.
'money' is uncountable, so 'so much ... that ...'.

items.stem: You like chicken rice, ____?

explain.why: 'like' uses 'do', so the tag needs 'don't', not 'aren't'.
The sentence is in the present, so the tag needs 'don't', not past 'didn't'.
The statement is positive, so the tag must be negative.

solution: You like chicken rice, don't you?
Positive present statement with 'like': the tag is 'don't you'.

items.stem: Ben can swim, ____?

explain.why: The statement has the modal 'can', so the tag needs 'can't', not 'isn't'.
The statement is positive, so the tag must be negative.
The statement uses 'can', so the tag repeats 'can', not 'does'.

solution: Ben can swim, can't he?
The tag repeats the modal 'can' in the opposite polarity: can't he.

items.stem: The pupils aren't late, ____?

explain.why: The statement is negative, so the tag must be positive.
'The pupils' is plural, so the pronoun must be 'they', not 'it'.
The statement uses 'are', so the tag repeats 'are', not 'do'.

solution: The pupils aren't late, are they?
Negative statement with 'are': the tag is positive 'are they'.

items.stem: Let's go to the library after school, ____?

explain.why: 'let us' is not a question tag.
After 'Let's' the tag is 'shall we', not a negative 'don't we'.
After 'Let's', the tag is 'shall we'.

solution: Let's go to the library after school, shall we?
'Let's ...' takes the tag 'shall we?'.

items.stem: She didn't finish her homework, ____?

explain.why: The statement is past, so the tag must use 'did', not 'does'.
The statement uses 'didn't', so the tag repeats 'did', not 'is'.
The statement has 'didn't', so the tag uses 'did', not 'had'.

solution: She didn't finish her homework, did she?
Negative past statement: the tag is positive 'did she'.

items.stem: Everyone is ready for the performance, ____?

explain.why: The statement is present ('is'), so the tag cannot be past 'weren't'.
The statement is positive, so the tag must be negative.
The statement uses 'is', so the tag repeats 'be' as 'aren't', not 'don't'.

solution: Everyone is ready for the performance, aren't they?
'Everyone' takes 'they' in the tag; positive statement gives negative 'aren't they'.

items.stem: I am the tallest in the class, ____?

explain.why: The statement uses 'am', so the tag uses 'be', not 'do'.
The statement uses 'am', so the tag uses 'be', not 'have'.
The subject is 'I', so the tag pronoun must be 'I', not 'it'.

solution: I am the tallest in the class, aren't I?
After 'I am', the standard tag is 'aren't I'.

items.stem: Nothing was wrong with the lift, ____?

explain.why: 'Nothing' makes the statement negative, so the tag must be positive, and the pronoun should be 'it'.
'Nothing' makes the statement negative, so the tag must be positive.
The statement is past ('was'), so the tag needs 'was', not 'is'.

solution: Nothing was wrong with the lift, was it?
'Nothing' is a negative word, so the tag is positive: was it.

items.stem: There is a queue outside the shop, ____?

explain.why: After 'There is', the tag repeats 'there', not 'it'.
'There is' is singular, so the tag uses 'isn't', not 'aren't'.
The statement is positive, so the tag must be negative.

solution: There is a queue outside the shop, isn't there?
'There is ...' takes the tag 'isn't there'.

items.stem: Your parents have never been to Sentosa, ____?

explain.why: The statement is present perfect, so the tag needs 'have', not 'had'.
The statement uses 'have', so the tag repeats 'have', not 'did'.
'never' makes the statement negative, so the tag must be positive.

solution: Your parents have never been to Sentosa, have they?
'never' is negative, so the tag is positive: have they.

items.stem: She used to take the school bus, ____?

explain.why: 'used to take' has no 'was', so 'wasn't' does not fit.
'used to' takes the past 'did' in the tag, not 'usedn't'.
'used to' is past, so the tag needs 'didn't', not 'doesn't'.

solution: She used to take the school bus, didn't she?
'used to' takes 'didn't' in the tag.

items.stem: You wouldn't mind waiting outside, ____?

explain.why: The statement is negative, so the tag must be positive.
The statement has the modal 'would', so the tag repeats 'would'.
The statement has 'would', so the tag repeats 'would', not 'will'.

solution: You wouldn't mind waiting outside, would you?
The tag repeats 'would' in the opposite polarity: would you.

items.stem: Hardly anyone came to the meeting, ____?

explain.why: 'anyone' is referred to with 'they' in a tag, not 'he'.
'Hardly' is negative, so the tag must be positive, and 'anyone' takes 'they'.
'Hardly' makes the statement negative, so the tag must be positive.

solution: Hardly anyone came to the meeting, did they?
'Hardly' is a negative word, so the tag is positive: did they.

items.stem: Neither of them wanted to join the CCA, ____?

explain.why: 'Neither of them' refers to people, so the tag pronoun is 'they', not 'it'.
'Neither' makes the statement negative, so the tag must be positive.
The statement is past ('wanted'), so the tag needs 'did', not 'do'.

solution: Neither of them wanted to join the CCA, did they?
'Neither' is negative, so the tag is positive: did they.

items.stem: We stayed indoors ____ it was raining heavily.

explain.why: 'although' shows contrast, but the rain is the reason.
'so' introduces a result, but 'it was raining' is the cause.
'unless' means 'if not', which does not fit a past reason.

solution: We stayed indoors because it was raining heavily.
The rain is the reason, so use 'because'.

items.stem: I wanted to buy the toy, ____ I did not have enough money.

explain.why: 'or' shows a choice, not a contrast.
'because' would say that wanting the toy was caused by having no money.
'so' shows result, but not having money is a contrast to wanting.

solution: I wanted to buy the toy, but I did not have enough money.
Contrast between wanting and being unable: 'but'.

items.stem: Please wash your hands ____ you eat.

explain.why: 'although' shows contrast, but this is a sequence.
'unless' means 'if not', which does not fit the sequence of washing and eating.
'so' shows result and cannot join the two actions this way.

solution: Please wash your hands before you eat.
Washing comes first, then eating: 'before'.

items.stem: ____ it was very hot, we played outside.

explain.why: 'Because' would make the heat the reason for playing outside.
'Nevertheless' links separate sentences; it is not a conjunction that joins the clause 'it was very hot' to the next one.
'But' joins two clauses and cannot begin a sentence like this, where 'it was very hot' is the contrast clause.

solution: Although it was very hot, we played outside.
A contrast at the start of the sentence: 'Although it was very hot, we played outside.'

items.stem: Hurry up, ____ you will miss the bus.

explain.why: 'but' shows contrast, not a warning of a result.
'so' would say that missing the bus is the aim of hurrying.
'and' would say that hurrying causes missing the bus.

solution: Hurry up, or you will miss the bus.
A command followed by a warning: 'or'.

items.stem: You cannot enter the lab ____ you wear safety goggles.

explain.why: 'though' shows contrast, not a condition.
'if' would say you cannot enter when you wear goggles, which is the opposite.
'as' gives a reason and does not state a condition.

solution: You cannot enter the lab unless you wear safety goggles.
'unless' means 'if you do not': cannot enter unless you wear goggles.

items.stem: He worked hard; ____, he did not pass the test.

explain.why: 'therefore' shows result, but failing is the opposite of what was expected.
'besides' adds a point and does not show contrast.
'moreover' adds a similar point, not a contrast.

solution: He worked hard; however, he did not pass the test.
A contrast between two sentences needs 'however'.

items.stem: The stall was closed; ____, we went to another one.

explain.why: 'otherwise' means 'if not', which does not fit a past event.
'nevertheless' shows contrast, but going elsewhere is a result.
'however' shows contrast, but going elsewhere is a result.

solution: The stall was closed; therefore, we went to another one.
The closing caused the choice, so 'therefore'.

items.stem: Not only did she win the race, ____ she also broke the school record.

explain.why: 'Not only' pairs with 'but', not 'or'.
'Not only' pairs with 'but', not 'and'.
'Not only' pairs with 'but', not 'so'.

solution: Not only did she win the race, but she also broke the school record.
'not only ... but also ...' is a fixed pair.

items.stem: I will wait here ____ you come back.

explain.why: 'unless' means 'if not', which does not fit waiting up to a time.
'because' gives a reason, but the sentence gives a time limit.
'since' looks back to a past starting point, but this is about the future.

solution: I will wait here until you come back.
Waiting up to a time takes 'until'.

items.stem: ____ the heavy rain, the match was not cancelled.

explain.why: 'Because' would give a reason for not cancelling, which is the wrong logic.
'However' links separate sentences and cannot start a phrase like this.
'Although' must be followed by a clause, but 'the heavy rain' is a noun phrase.

solution: Despite the heavy rain, the match was not cancelled.
'Despite' + noun phrase shows contrast.

items.stem: The school fair was a success ____ the poor weather.

explain.why: 'because of' would say the weather caused the success.
'even though' must be followed by a clause, not a noun phrase.
'although' must be followed by a clause, not a noun phrase.

solution: The school fair was a success in spite of the poor weather.
'in spite of' + noun phrase shows contrast.

items.stem: He studied hard ____ that he could pass the test.

explain.why: 'such that' is a different pattern and does not express purpose here.
'as that' is not a pattern for purpose; 'so that' is needed.
'very that' is not a correct pattern.

solution: He studied hard so that he could pass the test.
'so that' expresses purpose.

items.stem: Rina ran so fast ____ she overtook all the other runners.

explain.why: 'than' is used with comparatives, not with 'so ... '.
'so fast as' is used for comparison, not a result.
'so fast ____' needs 'that' to show the result, not 'which'.

solution: Rina ran so fast that she overtook all the other runners.
'so + adjective/adverb + that + result'.

items.stem: The girl ____ sits beside me is my cousin.

explain.why: 'whose' shows possession and needs a noun after it, but here it is followed by the verb 'sits'.
'which' is for things, but 'The girl' is a person.
'why' asks for a reason and cannot refer back to 'The girl'.

solution: The girl who sits beside me is my cousin.
For a person as subject, use 'who'.

items.stem: This is the book ____ I borrowed from the library.

explain.why: 'who' is for people, but 'book' is a thing.
'whose' shows possession, but the clause is about the thing that was borrowed.
'where' is used for places, but 'book' is not a place.

solution: This is the book that I borrowed from the library.
For a thing as object, use 'that' (or 'which').

items.stem: That is the boy ____ bicycle was stolen.

explain.why: 'whom' cannot show possession.
'which' is for things, but 'the boy' is a person.
'who' cannot be followed directly by the noun 'bicycle'; possession needs 'whose'.

solution: That is the boy whose bicycle was stolen.
Possession by a person: 'whose bicycle'.

items.stem: The hawker centre ____ we have lunch every Friday is very crowded.

explain.why: 'whose' shows possession, but the clause tells where we have lunch.
'which' would need a preposition, as in 'at which', to show the place.
'who' is for people, but 'hawker centre' is a place.

solution: The hawker centre where we have lunch every Friday is very crowded.
A place where an action happens takes 'where'.

items.stem: I do not know ____ left the lights on.

explain.why: 'whom' is for the object, but here the unknown person is the subject of 'left'.
'why' asks for a reason, but 'left' needs a subject that tells who left.
'whose' needs a noun after it to show ownership.

solution: I do not know who left the lights on.
The missing person is the subject of 'left', so 'who'.

items.stem: Mrs Lee, ____ taught me in Primary 4, retired last year.

explain.why: 'whom' is for the object, but Mrs Lee is the subject of 'taught'.
'whose' needs a noun after it, but 'taught' follows.
'she' repeats the subject instead of joining the clauses; a relative pronoun is needed.

solution: Mrs Lee, who taught me in Primary 4, retired last year.
Extra information about a named person, subject of the clause: 'who'.

items.stem: The pupil to ____ I lent my pencil case forgot to return it.

explain.why: 'whose' shows possession, but the clause is about who received the pencil case.
After a preposition ('to'), 'whom' is used, not 'who'.
'which' is for things, but 'The pupil' is a person.

solution: The pupil to whom I lent my pencil case forgot to return it.
After a preposition, use 'whom' for a person.

items.stem: She told us about the trip, ____ we found very interesting.

explain.why: 'what' cannot add information about the trip after a comma.
'whose' shows possession and needs a noun after it, but the clause is not about owning.
'that' is not used after a comma to add extra information.

solution: She told us about the trip, which we found very interesting.
After a comma, extra information about a thing takes 'which'.

items.stem: He asked me ____ I would like to join the chess club.

explain.why: 'what' would need to be the object of 'join', but 'to join the chess club' already has its object.
'whatever' does not introduce a yes/no reported question.
'asked me that' does not introduce a yes/no question.

solution: He asked me whether I would like to join the chess club.
A yes/no reported question uses 'whether' (or 'if').

items.stem: Everything ____ the guide told us about the old temple was fascinating.

explain.why: 'whose' shows possession, but the clause is not about owning.
'what' cannot follow 'Everything'; after 'everything' use 'that'.
'who' is for people, but 'Everything' is not a person.

solution: Everything that the guide told us about the old temple was fascinating.
After 'everything', the relative pronoun is 'that'.

items.stem: Ali hurt ____ while playing basketball.

explain.why: The subject and object are the same person, so the reflexive 'himself' is needed.
'his' is a possessive and needs a noun after it.
'Ali' is one person, so 'themselves' does not agree.

solution: Ali hurt himself while playing basketball.
When the object is the same person as the subject, use the reflexive: himself.

items.stem: Ali and Ben forgot ____ lunch boxes at home.

explain.why: 'they' is a subject pronoun and cannot come before a noun to show ownership.
'theirs' stands alone and cannot come before a noun.
'them' is an object pronoun and cannot come before a noun to show ownership.

solution: Ali and Ben forgot their lunch boxes at home.
A possessive determiner before a noun: their lunch boxes.

items.stem: That pencil case is not mine; it belongs to Siti. It is ____.

explain.why: 'her' must be followed by a noun; without one, use 'hers'.
'she' is a subject pronoun, but the blank needs a possessive.
'herself' means she did something to herself, not ownership.

solution: That pencil case is not mine; it belongs to Siti. It is hers.
A possessive pronoun that stands alone: hers.

items.stem: Between you and ____, I think the quiz will be difficult.

explain.why: After the preposition 'between', an object pronoun 'me' is needed, not 'I'.
'myself' is used only when 'I' is the subject of the same clause.
'mine' is a possessive pronoun, not an object after 'between'.

solution: Between you and me, I think the quiz will be difficult.
A pronoun after a preposition takes the object form: between you and me.

items.stem: The teacher asked the pupils to do the task by ____, without any help.

explain.why: 'theirs' is a possessive pronoun and does not mean 'alone'.
'their' is a possessive determiner and needs a noun after it.
'their own selves' is not the standard phrase; the idiom is 'by themselves'.

solution: The teacher asked the pupils to do the task by themselves, without any help.
'by + reflexive' means alone: by themselves.

items.stem: The puppy kept chasing ____ tail round the garden.

explain.why: 'it' cannot come before a noun to show ownership; the possessive form is needed.
'it's' means 'it is' or 'it has'; the possessive is 'its'.
The puppy is one animal, so 'their' does not agree.

solution: The puppy kept chasing its tail round the garden.
The possessive of 'it' has no apostrophe: its tail.

items.stem: Nobody except Tom and ____ knew about the surprise.

explain.why: 'except' is a preposition, so the object pronoun 'me' is needed, not 'I'.
'mine' is a possessive pronoun, not an object after 'except'.
'myself' cannot be used when there is no 'I' as the subject of the clause.

solution: Nobody except Tom and me knew about the surprise.
After 'except', use the object form: Tom and me.

items.stem: The principal praised Kai Xin and ____ for helping to organise the fair.

explain.why: 'mine' is a possessive pronoun and cannot be the object of 'praised'.
'myself' is used when the subject is 'I', but the subject here is 'The principal'.
'I' is a subject pronoun, but here the pronoun is the object of 'praised'.

solution: The principal praised Kai Xin and me for helping to organise the fair.
The object of 'praised' takes the object form: Kai Xin and me.

items.stem: You ____ wear your school badge every day.

explain.why: 'might' shows a weak possibility, not a rule.
'may' gives permission or shows a possibility, but a school rule needs 'must'.
'could' shows ability or possibility, not an obligation.

solution: You must wear your school badge every day.
A rule or duty uses 'must'.

items.stem: ____ I borrow your eraser, please?

explain.why: 'Do I borrow' asks about a habit, not permission.
'Shall I borrow' does not ask permission to take something.
'Would I borrow' asks about a possible situation, not permission.

solution: May I borrow your eraser, please?
Asking permission politely uses 'May I'.

items.stem: You ____ run along the corridor; it is dangerous.

explain.why: 'couldn't' shows past inability or doubt, not a rule.
'wouldn't' shows an unwillingness or a hypothetical, not a prohibition.
'needn't' means 'it is not necessary', but running is forbidden.

solution: You mustn't run along the corridor; it is dangerous.
A prohibition uses 'mustn't'.

items.stem: The lights are off, so the shop ____ be closed.

explain.why: 'shall' is used for offers or suggestions, not for guessing.
'can be closed' does not express a strong guess from evidence.
'would be closed' does not express a conclusion from evidence.

solution: The lights are off, so the shop must be closed.
A strong conclusion from evidence uses 'must'.

items.stem: You ____ bring an umbrella; the forecast says it will be sunny all day.

explain.why: 'mustn't' would forbid bringing an umbrella, but it is only unnecessary.
'couldn't' shows inability, not lack of need.
'wouldn't bring' does not say there is no need.

solution: You needn't bring an umbrella; the forecast says it will be sunny all day.
No need to do something uses 'needn't'.

items.stem: When I was young, I ____ swim, but now I swim like a fish.

explain.why: 'needn't' means 'no need to', not inability.
'shouldn't' gives advice and does not describe a past inability.
'can't' is present, but 'when I was young' needs the past.

solution: When I was young, I couldn't swim, but now I swim like a fish.
Past inability uses 'couldn't'.

items.stem: If you had told me earlier, I ____ have helped you.

explain.why: 'can have helped' does not fit a past unreal condition.
'will have' does not fit a past unreal condition.
'shall have helped' is not used in an unreal past condition.

solution: If you had told me earlier, I would have helped you.
A past unreal condition ('had told') takes 'would have' in the result.

items.stem: If it rains tomorrow, we ____ the picnic.

explain.why: 'would cancel' belongs to an unlikely situation, but a rainy day tomorrow is a real possibility.
The simple past 'cancelled' does not fit a future real possibility.
'had cancelled' is past perfect and does not fit a future situation.

solution: If it rains tomorrow, we will cancel the picnic.
Real possibility: 'If' + present, 'will' + verb.

items.stem: If I were you, I ____ the teacher for help.

explain.why: The result of an imaginary condition needs 'would', not the simple past.
'had asked' is past perfect and does not fit this present imaginary situation.
'If I were you' is an imaginary situation, so 'would' is needed, not 'will'.

solution: If I were you, I would ask the teacher for help.
Imaginary present condition: 'If I were', 'would' + verb.

items.stem: If the bus had come earlier, we ____ late for the show.

explain.why: The result clause needs 'would not have been', not past perfect.
'would not have being' is wrong; the participle needed is 'been'.
'will not be' is a future form and does not fit a condition about the past.

solution: If the bus had come earlier, we would not have been late for the show.
Past unreal condition: 'If' + past perfect, 'would have' + participle.

items.stem: Unless you ____ faster, you will miss the bus.

explain.why: A real future condition needs the simple present, not the simple past.
'unless' already means 'if not', so adding 'not' makes a double negative.
After 'unless', the verb stays in the present, not 'will'.

solution: Unless you run faster, you will miss the bus.
'Unless' + simple present (positive form): Unless you run faster ...

items.stem: If only I ____ more time yesterday, I would have finished the project.

explain.why: Present perfect 'have had' does not fit a condition about yesterday.
'would have' belongs in the result clause, not in the 'if' clause.
The past unreal condition needs 'had had' (past perfect of 'have'), not just 'had'.

solution: If only I had had more time yesterday, I would have finished the project.
Past unreal condition: 'had' + past participle, here 'had had'.

items.stem: I would not have been scolded if I ____ my homework.

explain.why: 'would do' belongs in the result clause, not after 'if'.
A past unreal condition needs past perfect, not the simple past.
'have done' does not fit a condition about the past.

solution: I would not have been scolded if I had done my homework.
Past unreal condition: 'if' + past perfect: had done.
